title: Book 5, Chapter 16 — Feeling against Sparta in Peloponnese—League of the Mantineans, Eleans, Argives, and Athenians—Battle of Mantinea and breaking up of the League
paragraphs: After the treaty and the alliance between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, concluded after the ten years' war in the ephorate of Pleistolas at Lacedaemon and the archonship of Alcaeus at Athens, the states that had accepted them were at peace. But the Corinthians and some of the cities in the Peloponnese tried to disturb the settlement, and a fresh agitation was instantly begun by the allies against Lacedaemon. Further, as time went on, the Lacedaemonians fell under suspicion at Athens for not carrying out some of the provisions of the treaty. Although for six years and ten months they refrained from invading each other's territory, abroad an unstable armistice did not prevent either party from doing the other the most effective injury, until they were finally forced to break the treaty made after the ten years' war and resort to open hostilities.

The history of this period has likewise been written by the same Thucydides, an Athenian, in the chronological order of events by summers and winters, down to the time when the Lacedaemonians and their allies put an end to the Athenian empire and took the Long Walls and Piraeus. The war by then had lasted twenty-seven years in all. Only a mistaken judgment can object to including the interval of treaty in the war. Looked at by the light of the facts, it cannot rationally be considered a state of peace — neither side either gave back or received all that they had agreed; and beyond that there were the violations on both sides in the Mantinean and Epidaurian wars and other instances, the fact that the allies in the direction of Thrace were as openly hostile as ever, and the fact that the Boeotians had only a truce that had to be renewed every ten days. So the first ten years' war, the treacherous armistice that followed it, and the subsequent war will, calculated by the seasons, be found to make up the number of years I have mentioned, with a difference of only a few days. They also offer an instance in which faith in oracles was, for once, justified by the event. I distinctly remember that throughout the war, from beginning to end, it was commonly declared that it would last thrice nine years. I lived through the whole of it, of an age to comprehend events, and giving my attention to them in order to know the exact truth. It was also my fate to be in exile from my country for twenty years after my command at Amphipolis. Being present with both sides, and especially with the Peloponnesians on account of my exile, I had leisure to observe affairs in some detail. I will accordingly now relate the disagreements that arose after the ten years' war, the breach of the treaty, and the hostilities that followed.

After the conclusion of the fifty years' truce and of the subsequent alliance, the embassies from the Peloponnese that had been summoned for this business returned from Lacedaemon. The rest went straight home, but the Corinthians first turned aside to Argos and opened negotiations with some of the men in office there. They argued that Lacedaemon could have no good end in view but the subjugation of the Peloponnese, otherwise she would never have entered into a treaty and alliance with the once-detested Athenians. The duty of looking out for the safety of the Peloponnese, they said, had now fallen on Argos. She should immediately pass a decree inviting any Hellenic state — provided it was independent and accustomed to meet fellow powers on the fair and equal ground of law and justice — to make a defensive alliance with the Argives. They proposed appointing a few individuals with full powers to negotiate, instead of going through the people, so that if any applicant were rejected, the fact of his approach would not become public. They said that many states would come over out of hatred for the Lacedaemonians. Having thus explained their views, the Corinthians returned home.

The persons they had communicated with reported the proposal to their government and people, and the Argives passed the decree and chose twelve men to negotiate an alliance for any Hellenic state that wished it, except Athens and Lacedaemon, neither of which could be admitted without reference to the Argive people. Argos came into the plan all the more readily because she saw that war with Lacedaemon was inevitable, the truce being on the point of expiring, and also because she hoped to gain the supremacy of the Peloponnese. For at this time Lacedaemon had sunk very low in public estimation because of her disasters, while the Argives were in a most flourishing condition, having taken no part in the Attic war and having on the contrary profited largely from their neutrality. The Argives accordingly prepared to receive into alliance any of the Hellenes who wished it.

The Mantineans and their allies were the first to come over, out of fear of the Lacedaemonians. Having taken advantage of the war against Athens to reduce a large part of Arcadia under their control, they thought Lacedaemon would not leave them undisturbed in their conquests now that she had time to interfere. So they gladly turned to a powerful city like Argos — the historical enemy of the Lacedaemonians, and a sister democracy. With the defection of Mantinea, the rest of the Peloponnese at once began to discuss the wisdom of following her example, supposing that the Mantineans could not have changed sides without good reason. Besides, they were angry with Lacedaemon, among other reasons, for having inserted in the treaty with Athens the clause that it should be consistent with their oaths for both parties — Lacedaemonians and Athenians — to add to or take away from it according to their discretion. It was this clause that was the real origin of the panic in the Peloponnese, since it raised suspicions of a Lacedaemonian and Athenian combination against their liberties. Properly, any alteration should have been made conditional on the consent of the whole body of allies. With these fears, there was a very general desire in each state to enter into alliance with Argos.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians, perceiving the agitation going on in the Peloponnese — that Corinth was the author of it and was herself about to enter into alliance with the Argives — sent ambassadors there in the hope of preventing what was being planned. They accused Corinth of having brought it all about, and told her she could not desert Lacedaemon and become an ally of Argos without adding violation of her oaths to the offence she had already committed in not accepting the treaty with Athens, when it had been expressly agreed that the decision of the majority of the allies should be binding, unless the gods or heroes stood in the way. Corinth, in her answer, delivered before those of her allies who had like her refused to accept the treaty and whom she had previously invited to attend, refrained from openly stating the injuries she complained of — such as the non-recovery of Sollium or Anactorium from the Athenians, or any other point on which she thought she had been wronged. She took shelter under the pretext that she could not give up her Thracian allies, to whom her separate individual security had been given when they first revolted with Potidæa, as well as on subsequent occasions. She therefore denied that she committed any violation of her oaths to the allies in not entering the treaty with Athens. Having sworn upon the faith of the gods to her Thracian friends, she could not honestly give them up. Besides, the formula was "unless the gods or heroes stand in the way." And here, as it appeared to her, the gods stood in the way. This was what she said on the matter of her former oaths. As to the Argive alliance, she would consult with her friends and do whatever was right. The Lacedaemonian envoys returned home. Some Argive ambassadors who happened to be in Corinth pressed her to conclude the alliance without further delay, but were told to attend at the next congress to be held at Corinth.

Immediately afterwards an Elean embassy arrived. Having first made an alliance with Corinth, they went on from there to Argos, according to their instructions, and became allies of the Argives, their country being just then at enmity with Lacedaemon and Lepreum. Some time before, there had been a war between the Lepreans and some of the Arcadians. The Eleans, called in by the Lepreans with the offer of half their lands, had ended the war, leaving the land in the hands of its Leprean occupiers but imposing on them the tribute of a talent to Olympian Zeus. Until the Attic war this tribute was paid by the Lepreans, who then took the war as an excuse to stop paying. When the Eleans used force, the Lepreans appealed to Lacedaemon. The case was thus submitted to her arbitration, but the Eleans, suspecting the fairness of the tribunal, withdrew the reference and laid waste the Leprean territory. The Lacedaemonians nevertheless decided that the Lepreans were independent and the Eleans the aggressors, and as the Eleans did not abide by the arbitration, they sent a garrison of heavy infantry into Lepreum. At this the Eleans, holding that Lacedaemon had received one of their rebel subjects, invoked the convention providing that each confederate should come out of the Attic war in possession of what he had when he went into it. Considering that justice had not been done them, they went over to the Argives, and now made the alliance through their ambassadors, who had been instructed for the purpose. Immediately after them the Corinthians and the Thracian Chalcidians became allies of Argos. Meanwhile the Boeotians and Megarians, who acted together, kept quiet, being left to do as they pleased by Lacedaemon, and thinking that the Argive democracy would not suit their aristocratic government as well as the Lacedaemonian constitution.

About the same time in this summer, Athens succeeded in reducing Scione, put the adult males to death, made slaves of the women and children, and gave the land for the Plataeans to live in. She also brought the Delians back to Delos, moved by her misfortunes in the field and by the commands of the god at Delphi. Meanwhile the Phocians and Locrians began hostilities. The Corinthians and Argives, now in alliance, went to Tegea to bring about its defection from Lacedaemon, seeing that if so considerable a state could be persuaded to join, all the Peloponnese would be with them. But when the Tegeans said they would do nothing against Lacedaemon, the previously zealous Corinthians slackened their efforts and began to fear that none of the rest would now come over. Still they went to the Boeotians and tried to persuade them to alliance and joint action with Argos and themselves, and also begged them to come with them to Athens to obtain a ten-day truce of the kind that had been made between the Athenians and Boeotians not long after the fifty years' treaty. If the Athenians refused, the Boeotians were to throw up their armistice and not make any future truce without Corinth. These were the requests of the Corinthians. The Boeotians put them off on the matter of the Argive alliance, but went with them to Athens, where, however, they failed to obtain the ten-day truce — the Athenians' answer being that the Corinthians already had one, as allies of Lacedaemon. Nevertheless the Boeotians did not throw up their ten-day truce, despite the Corinthians' prayers and reproaches at this breach of faith. The Corinthians had to content themselves with a de facto armistice with Athens.

The same summer the Lacedaemonians marched into Arcadia with their whole levy under Pleistoanax, son of Pausanias, king of Lacedaemon, against the Parrhasians, who were subjects of Mantinea, and a faction among whom had asked for their help. They also intended to demolish, if possible, the fort at Cypsela that the Mantineans had built and garrisoned in Parrhasian territory to harass the district of Sciritis in Laconia. The Lacedaemonians accordingly laid waste the Parrhasian country, and the Mantineans, placing their town in the hands of an Argive garrison, set about defending their confederacy. Unable to save Cypsela or the Parrhasian towns, they returned to Mantinea. Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians declared the Parrhasians independent, razed the fortress, and went home.

The same summer the soldiers from Thrace who had gone out with Brasidas came back, having been brought from there after the treaty by Clearidas. The Lacedaemonians decreed that the Helots who had fought with Brasidas should be free and allowed to live wherever they liked, and not long afterward settled them with the Neodamodes at Lepreum, on the Laconian-Elean border — Lacedaemon being at the time at enmity with Elis. Those Spartans who had been taken prisoner on the island and surrendered their arms might, it was feared, suppose they were to be subjected to some degradation as a result of their misfortune, and so attempt some kind of revolution if left in possession of their full citizenship. They were therefore at once disfranchised, even though some of them were in office at the time, and were thus disqualified from holding office or buying and selling anything. After some time, however, their citizen rights were restored.

The same summer the Dians took Thyssus, a town on Acte by Athos in alliance with Athens. Throughout the whole of this summer relations between the Athenians and Peloponnesians continued, although each side began to suspect the other immediately after the treaty, because the places named in it had not been restored. Lacedaemon, whose lot it was to begin by giving back Amphipolis and the other towns, had not done so. She had equally failed to get the treaty accepted by her Thracian allies, or by the Boeotians or Corinthians, although she was continually promising to join with Athens in compelling their compliance if it were any longer refused. She kept fixing dates after which those who still refused to come in were to be declared enemies to both sides, but took care not to bind herself by any written agreement. Meanwhile the Athenians, seeing none of these professions actually carried out, began to suspect the honesty of her intentions. Consequently they not only refused to comply with her demands for Pylos but also regretted having given up the prisoners from the island, and held tight to the other places until Lacedaemon had fulfilled her part of the treaty. Lacedaemon, on her part, said she had done what she could: she had given up the Athenian prisoners of war in her possession, evacuated Thrace, and performed everything else within her power. Restoring Amphipolis was beyond her ability, but she would try to bring the Boeotians and Corinthians into the treaty, to recover Panactum, and to send home all the Athenian prisoners of war in Boeotia. Meanwhile she required that Pylos be restored, or at any rate that the Messenians and Helots be withdrawn — as her own troops had been from Thrace — and the place garrisoned, if necessary, by the Athenians themselves. After a number of conferences during the summer, she succeeded in persuading Athens to withdraw from Pylos the Messenians and the rest of the Helots and deserters from Laconia, who were accordingly settled by her at Cranii in Cephallenia. Thus during this summer there was peace and intercourse between the two peoples.

Next winter, however, the ephors under whom the treaty had been made were no longer in office, and some of their successors were directly opposed to it. Embassies now arrived from the Lacedaemonian confederacy, and the Athenians, Boeotians, and Corinthians also presented themselves at Lacedaemon. After much discussion and no agreement, they separated for their several homes. Cleobulus and Xenares, the two ephors most anxious to break off the treaty, took advantage of this to confer privately with the Boeotians and Corinthians. They advised them to act together as much as possible, and instructed the Boeotians first to enter into alliance with Argos, and then try to bring themselves and the Argives into alliance with Lacedaemon. The Boeotians would in this way be least likely to be forced into the Attic treaty, while the Lacedaemonians would prefer to gain the friendship and alliance of Argos even at the price of war with Athens and the rupture of the treaty. The Boeotians knew that an honorable friendship with Argos had long been desired by Lacedaemon, since the Lacedaemonians believed that this would significantly facilitate the conduct of the war outside the Peloponnese. Meanwhile they begged the Boeotians to put Panactum into Lacedaemonian hands, so that she might if possible obtain Pylos in exchange for it, and so be in a better position to resume hostilities with Athens.

After receiving these instructions for their governments from Xenares and Cleobulus and their friends at Lacedaemon, the Boeotians and Corinthians departed. On their way home they were joined by two persons high in office at Argos, who had been waiting for them on the road, and who now sounded them on the possibility of the Boeotians joining the Corinthians, Eleans, and Mantineans in becoming allies of Argos — on the idea that, if this could be arranged, they would be able, thus united, to make peace or war as they pleased, against Lacedaemon or any other power. The Boeotian envoys were pleased to find themselves accidentally asked to do what their friends at Lacedaemon had told them to do. The two Argives, perceiving that their proposal was welcome, departed with a promise to send ambassadors to the Boeotians. On their arrival home, the Boeotians reported to the Boeotarchs what had been said to them at Lacedaemon and also by the Argives who had met them on the road. The Boeotarchs, pleased with the idea, embraced it all the more eagerly because of the lucky coincidence that Argos was asking for the very thing their friends at Lacedaemon had wanted. Shortly afterwards ambassadors arrived from Argos with the proposals indicated. The Boeotarchs approved of the terms and dismissed the ambassadors with a promise to send envoys to Argos to negotiate the alliance.

In the meantime it was decided by the Boeotarchs, the Corinthians, the Megarians, and the envoys from Thrace first to exchange oaths together — to give help to one another whenever required, and not to make war or peace except in common — after which the Boeotians and Megarians, who acted together, would make the alliance with Argos. But before the oaths were taken, the Boeotarchs communicated these proposals to the four councils of the Boeotians, in whom the supreme power resides, and advised them to exchange oaths with all such cities as should be willing to enter into a defensive league with the Boeotians. But the members of the Boeotian councils refused their consent, fearing to offend Lacedaemon by entering into a league with the deserter Corinth. The Boeotarchs had not informed them of what had passed at Lacedaemon, or of the advice given by Cleobulus and Xenares and the Boeotian partisans there — namely, that they should become allies of Corinth and Argos as a preliminary to a junction with Lacedaemon. They imagined that even without saying anything about this, the councils would not vote against what had been decided and recommended by the Boeotarchs. With this difficulty arising, the Corinthians and the envoys from Thrace departed without anything having been concluded. The Boeotarchs, who had previously intended after this to try to bring about the Argive alliance, now omitted to bring the Argive question before the councils, or to send to Argos the envoys whom they had promised. A general coldness and delay set in over the matter.
In the same winter Mecyberna, which had an Athenian garrison inside it, was assaulted and taken by the Olynthians.

All this while, negotiations had been going on between the Athenians and Lacedaemonians about the conquests still held by each. Lacedaemon, hoping that if Athens were to get back Panactum from the Boeotians she might herself recover Pylos, now sent an embassy to the Boeotians and begged them to put Panactum and their Athenian prisoners into her hands, so that she could exchange them for Pylos. The Boeotians refused unless Lacedaemon made a separate alliance with them, as she had with Athens. Lacedaemon knew that this would be a breach of faith to Athens, since it had been agreed that neither side would make peace or war without the other. But wishing to obtain Panactum, which she hoped to exchange for Pylos, and with the party that pressed for the dissolution of the treaty strongly favoring the Boeotian connection, she at length concluded the alliance just as winter gave way to spring. Panactum was instantly razed. And so the eleventh year of the war ended.

In the first days of the following summer, the Argives — seeing that the promised ambassadors from Boeotia did not arrive, that Panactum was being demolished, and that a separate alliance had been concluded between the Boeotians and Lacedaemonians — began to fear that Argos might be left isolated and the whole confederacy go over to Lacedaemon. They imagined that the Boeotians had been persuaded by the Lacedaemonians to raze Panactum and to enter into the treaty with the Athenians, and that Athens was privy to this arrangement, so that not even her alliance was open to them any longer — a resource they had always been counting on, given the existing dissensions, in case their treaty with Lacedaemon should not continue. In this strait the Argives, afraid that as a result of refusing to renew the treaty with Lacedaemon and aspiring to the supremacy of the Peloponnese, they would have the Lacedaemonians, Tegeans, Boeotians, and Athenians on their hands all at once, now hastily sent off Eustrophus and Aeson — who seemed the men most likely to be acceptable — as envoys to Lacedaemon, with the aim of making the best treaty they could with the Lacedaemonians on whatever terms they could get, and being left in peace.

On reaching Lacedaemon, their ambassadors began to negotiate the terms of the proposed treaty. What the Argives first asked was that they be allowed to refer to the arbitration of some state or private person the question of the Cynurian land — a piece of frontier territory about which they have always been disputing, which contains the towns of Thyrea and Anthene, and which is occupied by the Lacedaemonians. The Lacedaemonians at first said they could not allow this point to be discussed, but were ready to conclude on the old terms. Eventually, however, the Argive ambassadors got this concession from them. For the present there was to be a truce of fifty years; but if there were neither plague nor war in Lacedaemon or Argos, it should be open to either party to issue a formal challenge and decide the question of this territory by battle, as on a former occasion when both sides had claimed the victory — pursuit not being allowed beyond the frontier of Argos or Lacedaemon. The Lacedaemonians at first thought this sheer folly, but at length, anxious at any cost to have the friendship of Argos, they agreed to the terms demanded and put them in writing. However, before any of this should become binding, the ambassadors were to return to Argos and consult with their people. If approved, they were to come at the festival of the Hyacinthia and take the oaths.

The envoys returned accordingly. Meanwhile, while the Argives were engaged in these negotiations, the Lacedaemonian ambassadors — Andromedes, Phaedimus, and Antimenidas — who were to receive the prisoners from the Boeotians and restore them and Panactum to the Athenians, found that the Boeotians had themselves razed Panactum, on the plea that oaths had been anciently exchanged between their people and the Athenians, after a dispute on the subject, to the effect that neither should inhabit the place but they should graze it in common. As for the Athenian prisoners of war held by the Boeotians, these were handed over to Andromedes and his colleagues, who conveyed them to Athens and gave them back. The envoys at the same time announced the razing of Panactum, which to them seemed as good as its restitution, since it would no longer house an enemy of Athens. This announcement was received with great indignation by the Athenians, who thought the Lacedaemonians had played them false — both in the matter of the demolition of Panactum, which ought to have been restored to them standing, and in having, as they now learned, made a separate alliance with the Boeotians, in spite of their previous promise to join Athens in compelling the adhesion of those who refused to accede to the treaty. The Athenians also considered the other points on which Lacedaemon had failed in her compact, and thinking they had been duped, gave an angry answer to the ambassadors and sent them away.

With the breach between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians having gone this far, the party at Athens that wished to cancel the treaty also at once put themselves in motion. Foremost among these was Alcibiades, son of Clinias, a man still young in years for any other Hellenic city but distinguished by the splendor of his ancestry. Alcibiades thought the Argive alliance really preferable, though personal pique also had a great deal to do with his opposition. He was offended with the Lacedaemonians for having negotiated the treaty through Nicias and Laches and overlooked him on account of his youth, and also for not having shown him the respect due to his family's ancient connection with them as their proxeni — a connection his grandfather had renounced, and which he had himself lately thought to renew by his attentions to their prisoners taken on the island. Considering himself slighted on all sides, he had at first spoken against the treaty, saying the Lacedaemonians were not to be trusted, but that they were only treating in order to be enabled by this means to crush Argos, and afterwards to attack Athens alone. Now, immediately after the events above, he sent privately to the Argives, telling them to come as quickly as possible to Athens, accompanied by the Mantineans and Eleans, with proposals of alliance, since the moment was favorable and he himself would do all he could to help them.

On receiving this message and discovering that the Athenians, far from being in on the Boeotian alliance, were involved in a serious quarrel with the Lacedaemonians, the Argives paid no further attention to the embassy they had just sent to Lacedaemon about the treaty, and began to incline rather toward the Athenians. They reflected that, in the event of war, they would in this way have on their side a city that was not only an ancient ally of Argos but a sister democracy and very powerful at sea. They accordingly at once sent ambassadors to Athens to negotiate an alliance, accompanied by others from Elis and Mantinea.

At the same time an embassy arrived in haste from Lacedaemon, made up of men reputed to be well disposed toward the Athenians — Philocharidas, Leon, and Endius. They were sent for fear that the Athenians in their irritation might conclude an alliance with the Argives, and also to ask back Pylos in exchange for Panactum, and to plead in defence of the alliance with the Boeotians that it had not been made to harm the Athenians. When the envoys spoke in the senate on these points and stated that they had come with full powers to settle all matters at issue between the two states, Alcibiades became afraid that, if they repeated these statements to the popular assembly, they might win over the multitude and the Argive alliance might be rejected. So he had recourse to the following stratagem. He persuaded the Lacedaemonians by a solemn assurance that, if they would say nothing about their full powers in the assembly, he would give Pylos back to them — he himself, the present opponent of its restitution, undertaking to obtain this from the Athenians — and would settle the other points at issue. His plan was to detach them from Nicias and to disgrace them before the people as having no sincerity in their intentions, or even common consistency in their language, and so to get the Argives, Eleans, and Mantineans taken into alliance. The plan succeeded. When the envoys appeared before the people, and on the question being put to them did not say, as they had said in the senate, that they had come with full powers, the Athenians lost all patience. Carried away by Alcibiades, who thundered more loudly than ever against the Lacedaemonians, they were ready to introduce the Argives and their companions on the spot and take them into alliance. An earthquake occurred, however, before anything definite had been done, and this assembly was adjourned.

In the assembly held the next day, Nicias — in spite of the fact that the Lacedaemonians had been deceived themselves and had let him be deceived as well, by not admitting they had come with full powers — still maintained that the best course was to be friends with the Lacedaemonians, and, letting the Argive proposals stand over, to send once more to Lacedaemon and learn her intentions. The postponement of the war could only increase their own prestige and damage that of their rivals. The excellent state of their affairs made it their interest to preserve this prosperity as long as possible, while those of Lacedaemon were so desperate that the sooner she could try her fortune again, the better. He succeeded accordingly in persuading them to send ambassadors, himself among the number, to invite the Lacedaemonians, if they were really sincere, to restore Panactum intact along with Amphipolis, and to abandon their alliance with the Boeotians (unless they consented to accede to the treaty), in keeping with the stipulation that forbade either to treat without the other. The ambassadors were also instructed to say that the Athenians, had they wished to play false, might already have made an alliance with the Argives, who had indeed come to Athens for that very purpose. They went off furnished with instructions on any other complaints the Athenians had to make. On reaching Lacedaemon, they communicated their instructions, and concluded by telling the Lacedaemonians that unless they gave up their alliance with the Boeotians, in case the Boeotians did not accede to the treaty, the Athenians for their part would ally themselves with the Argives and their friends. The Lacedaemonians, however, refused to give up the Boeotian alliance — the party of Xenares the ephor and those who shared their view carrying the day on this point — but renewed the oaths at the request of Nicias, who feared to return without having accomplished anything and to be disgraced. That was indeed his fate, since he was held to be the author of the treaty with Lacedaemon. When he came back, and the Athenians heard that nothing had been done at Lacedaemon, they flew into a fury. Deciding that faith had not been kept with them, they took advantage of the presence of the Argives and their allies, who had been brought in by Alcibiades, and made a treaty and alliance with them on the following terms:
The Athenians, Argives, Mantineans, and Eleans, acting for themselves and the allies in their respective empires, made a treaty for a hundred years, to be without fraud or harm by land or by sea.

1. It shall not be lawful to make war, either for the Argives, Eleans, Mantineans, and their allies, against the Athenians or the allies in the Athenian empire; or for the Athenians and their allies against the Argives, Eleans, Mantineans, or their allies, in any way or by any means whatsoever.
The Athenians, Argives, Eleans, and Mantineans shall be allies for a hundred years on the following terms:

2. If an enemy invades the country of the Athenians, the Argives, Eleans, and Mantineans shall come to the aid of Athens, as the Athenians may require by message, in whatever way they can most effectively, to the best of their power. But if the invader has gone after plundering the territory, the offending state shall be the enemy of the Argives, Mantineans, Eleans, and Athenians, and war shall be made on it by all these cities. None of these cities may make peace with that state unless all of the above cities agree to do so.

3. Likewise the Athenians shall come to the aid of Argos, Mantinea, and Elis, if an enemy invades the country of Elis, Mantinea, or Argos, as the above cities may require by message, in whatever way they can most effectively, to the best of their power. But if the invader has gone after plundering the territory, the offending state shall be the enemy of the Athenians, Argives, Mantineans, and Eleans, and war shall be made on it by all these cities, and peace may not be made with that state unless all of the above cities agree to it.

4. No armed force shall be allowed to pass for hostile purposes through the country of the contracting powers, or of the allies in their respective empires, or to go by sea, except all of the cities — that is, Athens, Argos, Mantinea, and Elis — vote for such passage.

5. The relieving troops shall be maintained by the city sending them for thirty days from their arrival in the city that has called for them, and the same on their return. If their services are wanted for a longer period, the city that sent for them shall maintain them, at the rate of three Aeginetan obols a day for a heavy-armed soldier, archer, or light soldier, and an Aeginetan drachma for a trooper.

6. The city sending for the troops shall have the command when the war is in its own country. But if the cities decide on a joint expedition, the command shall be equally divided among all the cities.

7. The treaty shall be sworn to by the Athenians for themselves and their allies, and by the Argives, Mantineans, Eleans, and their allies, by each state individually. Each shall swear the oath most binding in his country over full-grown victims, the oath being as follows:
"I STAND BY THE ALLIANCE AND ITS ARTICLES, JUSTLY, INNOCENTLY, AND SINCERELY, AND I WILL NOT TRANSGRESS THEM IN ANY WAY OR BY ANY MEANS WHATSOEVER."

The oath shall be taken at Athens by the Senate and the magistrates, with the Prytanes administering it; at Argos by the Senate, the Eighty, and the Artynae, with the Eighty administering it; at Mantinea by the Demiurgi, the Senate, and the other magistrates, with the Theori and Polemarchs administering it; at Elis by the Demiurgi, the magistrates, and the Six Hundred, with the Demiurgi and the Thesmophylaces administering it. The oaths shall be renewed by the Athenians going to Elis, Mantinea, and Argos thirty days before the Olympic games, and by the Argives, Mantineans, and Eleans going to Athens ten days before the great festival of the Panathenaea. The articles of the treaty, the oaths, and the alliance shall be inscribed on a stone pillar by the Athenians on the citadel, by the Argives in the marketplace in the temple of Apollo, and by the Mantineans in the temple of Zeus in the marketplace. A bronze pillar shall be set up jointly by them at the Olympic games now at hand. Should the above cities see fit to make any addition to these articles, whatever all of the above cities agree on, after consulting together, shall be binding.

Although the treaty and alliances were thus concluded, the treaty between the Lacedaemonians and Athenians was not renounced by either side. Meanwhile Corinth, although an ally of the Argives, did not accede to the new treaty, any more than she had done to the alliance, defensive and offensive, formed earlier between the Eleans, Argives, and Mantineans, when she declared herself content with the first alliance, which was defensive only and bound them to help one another but not to join in attacking anyone. The Corinthians thus stood aloof from their allies, and again turned their thoughts toward Lacedaemon.

At the Olympic games held this summer, in which the Arcadian Androsthenes was victor for the first time in the wrestling and boxing, the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple by the Eleans, and thus prevented from sacrificing or competing, because they had refused to pay the fine specified in the Olympic law that the Eleans had imposed on them. The Eleans alleged that they had attacked Fort Phyrcus and had sent heavy infantry of theirs into Lepreum during the Olympic truce. The amount of the fine was two thousand minae — two for each heavy-armed soldier, as the law prescribes. The Lacedaemonians sent envoys and argued that the fine was unjust, claiming that the truce had not yet been proclaimed at Lacedaemon when the heavy infantry were sent off. But the Eleans maintained that the armistice with them had already begun (they proclaim it first among themselves) and that the Lacedaemonian aggression had taken them by surprise while they were living quietly as in peacetime, expecting nothing of the kind. The Lacedaemonians replied that, if the Eleans really believed they had committed aggression, it would have been pointless to proclaim the truce at Lacedaemon afterwards. But they had proclaimed it nonetheless, since they believed nothing of the kind, and from that moment the Lacedaemonians had made no attack on their country. The Eleans, however, stuck to what they had said, that nothing would persuade them that an aggression had not been committed. They added, however, that if the Lacedaemonians would restore Lepreum, they would give up their own share of the money and pay the god's share for them.

When this offer was not accepted, the Eleans tried a second. Instead of restoring Lepreum, if that was objected to, the Lacedaemonians should ascend the altar of Olympian Zeus, since they were so anxious to have access to the temple, and swear before the Hellenes that they would in fact pay the fine at a later date. This too was refused. So the Lacedaemonians were excluded from the temple, the sacrifice, and the games, and sacrificed at home, the Lepreans being the only other Hellenes who did not attend. Still the Eleans were afraid of the Lacedaemonians sacrificing by force, and kept watch with a company of heavy-armed young men. They were also joined by a thousand Argives, the same number of Mantineans, and some Athenian cavalry who stayed at Harpina during the festival. Great fears were felt in the assembly that the Lacedaemonians might come in arms, especially after Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, a Lacedaemonian, had been scourged on the course by the umpires. The reason was that, when his horses won and the Boeotian people were proclaimed the victors because he had no right to enter, he came forward on the course and crowned the charioteer, to show that the chariot was his. After this incident, everyone was more afraid than before, and confidently expected a disturbance. The Lacedaemonians, however, kept quiet and let the festival pass by, as we have seen. After the Olympic games, the Argives and the allies went to Corinth to invite her to come over to them. There they found some Lacedaemonian envoys, and a long discussion took place, which in the end came to nothing, as an earthquake occurred and they dispersed to their various homes.

Summer was now over. In the following winter a battle took place between the Heracleots in Trachinia and the Aenianians, Dolopians, Malians, and certain of the Thessalians — all tribes bordering on the town and hostile to it, since it directly threatened their country. Accordingly, having opposed and harassed it from its very foundation by every means in their power, they now in this battle defeated the Heracleots. Xenares, son of Cnidis, their Lacedaemonian commander, was among the slain. Thus the winter ended, and the twelfth year of this war also ended. After the battle, Heraclea was so terribly reduced that in the first days of the following summer the Boeotians occupied the place and sent away the Lacedaemonian Agesippidas for misgovernment, fearing that the town might be taken by the Athenians while the Lacedaemonians were distracted by the affairs of the Peloponnese. The Lacedaemonians, however, were offended with them for what they had done.

The same summer Alcibiades, son of Clinias, now one of the generals at Athens, acting in concert with the Argives and the allies, went into the Peloponnese with a few Athenian heavy infantry and archers and some of the allies in those parts whom he took up as he passed. With this army he marched here and there through the Peloponnese, settling various matters connected with the alliance. Among other things, he induced the Patrians to carry their walls down to the sea, intending himself also to build a fort near the Achaean Rhium. However, the Corinthians and Sicyonians, and all others who would have suffered by its being built, came up and stopped him.

The same summer war broke out between the Epidaurians and Argives. The pretext was that the Epidaurians had not sent an offering for their pasture-land to Apollo Pythaeus, as they were bound to do, the Argives having the chief management of the temple. But aside from this pretext, Alcibiades and the Argives were determined, if possible, to gain possession of Epidaurus, and so to secure the neutrality of Corinth and give the Athenians a shorter passage for their reinforcements from Aegina than if they had to sail around Scyllaeum. The Argives accordingly prepared to invade Epidaurus on their own, to exact the offering.

About the same time the Lacedaemonians marched out with their whole levy to Leuctra on their frontier, opposite Mount Lycaeum, under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus, without anyone knowing their destination, not even the cities that sent the contingents. The frontier sacrifices, however, did not prove favorable, so the Lacedaemonians themselves went home, and sent word to the allies to be ready to march after the coming month, which happened to be the month of Carneus, a sacred time for the Dorians. On the Lacedaemonian withdrawal the Argives marched out three days before the end of the month preceding Carneus, and keeping this as the date during the whole time they were in the field, they invaded and plundered Epidaurus. The Epidaurians summoned their allies for help. Some pleaded the holy month as an excuse; others came as far as the frontier of Epidaurus and stayed there inactive.

While the Argives were in Epidaurus, embassies from the cities assembled at Mantinea on the invitation of the Athenians. After the conference began, the Corinthian Euphamidas said that their actions did not match their words: while they sat deliberating about peace, the Epidaurians and their allies and the Argives were drawn up in arms against each other. Deputies from each side should first go and separate the armies, and only then could the talk about peace resume. In compliance with this suggestion they went and brought the Argives back from Epidaurus, then reassembled, but with no better success in reaching a conclusion. The Argives invaded Epidaurus a second time and plundered the country. The Lacedaemonians also marched out to Caryae, but the frontier sacrifices were again unfavorable, and they went back. After ravaging about a third of Epidaurian territory, the Argives returned home. Meanwhile a thousand Athenian heavy infantry had come to their aid under the command of Alcibiades, but finding that the Lacedaemonian expedition was over and their services no longer needed, they went back as well.

So passed the summer. The next winter the Lacedaemonians managed to elude the vigilance of the Athenians and slipped a garrison of three hundred men into Epidaurus by sea, under the command of Agesippidas. At this the Argives went to the Athenians and complained that they had allowed an enemy to pass by sea, in spite of the clause in the treaty by which the allies were not to allow an enemy to pass through their country. Unless the Athenians now put the Messenians and Helots into Pylos to harass the Lacedaemonians, the Argives said, they would consider that faith had not been kept with them. The Athenians were persuaded by Alcibiades to inscribe at the bottom of the Laconian pillar that the Lacedaemonians had not kept their oaths, and to convey the Helots at Cranii to Pylos to plunder the country. For the rest, however, they remained quiet as before. During this winter hostilities went on between the Argives and Epidaurians, with no pitched battle, only forays and ambushes in which the losses were small and fell now on one side, now on the other. At the close of the winter, toward the beginning of spring, the Argives went with scaling ladders to Epidaurus, expecting to find it left unguarded on account of the war and to take it by assault, but they returned unsuccessful. So the winter ended, and with it the thirteenth year of the war.

In the middle of the next summer the Lacedaemonians, seeing the Epidaurians, their allies, in distress, and the rest of the Peloponnese either in revolt or disaffected, concluded that it was high time for them to interfere if they wished to stop the spread of the trouble. Accordingly with their full force, including the Helots, they took the field against Argos, under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. The Tegeans and the other Arcadian allies of Lacedaemon joined the expedition. The allies from the rest of the Peloponnese and from outside it mustered at Phlius: the Boeotians with five thousand heavy infantry and as many light troops, plus five hundred horse and the same number of dismounted troopers; the Corinthians with two thousand heavy infantry; the rest more or less as it happened to come out; and the Phliasians with all their forces, since the army was in their country.

The Lacedaemonians' preparations had been known from the start to the Argives, who, however, did not take the field until the enemy was on his way to join the rest at Phlius. Reinforced by the Mantineans with their allies, and by three thousand Elean heavy infantry, they advanced and met the Lacedaemonians at Methydrium in Arcadia. Each side took up its position on a hill, and the Argives prepared to engage the Lacedaemonians while they were still alone. But Agis eluded them by breaking up his camp in the night and went on to join the rest of the allies at Phlius. The Argives, discovering this at daybreak, marched first to Argos and then to the Nemean road, by which they expected the Lacedaemonians and their allies would come down. Agis, however, instead of taking this road as they expected, gave the Lacedaemonians, Arcadians, and Epidaurians their orders, and went by another difficult road, descending into the plain of Argos. The Corinthians, Pellenians, and Phliasians marched by another steep road, while the Boeotians, Megarians, and Sicyonians had instructions to come down by the Nemean road where the Argives were posted, so that, if the enemy advanced into the plain against the troops of Agis, they might fall on his rear with their cavalry. With these dispositions made, Agis invaded the plain and began to ravage Saminthus and other places.

On discovering this the Argives came up from Nemea, day having now dawned. On the way they fell in with the troops of the Phliasians and Corinthians, killed a few of the Phliasians, and had perhaps a few more of their own men killed by the Corinthians. Meanwhile the Boeotians, Megarians, and Sicyonians, advancing on Nemea according to their instructions, found that the Argives were no longer there, having gone down on seeing their property ravaged, and were now forming for battle, the Lacedaemonians doing the same. The Argives were now completely surrounded. From the plain the Lacedaemonians and their allies cut them off from their city; above them were the Corinthians, Phliasians, and Pellenians; on the side of Nemea were the Boeotians, Sicyonians, and Megarians. Their army had no cavalry, since the Athenians alone among the allies had not yet arrived. Now the bulk of the Argives and their allies did not see the danger of their position, but thought they could not have a fairer field, since they had intercepted the Lacedaemonians in their own country and close to the city. Two men in the Argive army, however — Thrasylus, one of the five generals, and Alciphron, the Lacedaemonian proxenus — just as the armies were on the point of engaging went and parleyed with Agis. They urged him not to bring on a battle, on the grounds that the Argives were ready to refer whatever complaints the Lacedaemonians had against them to fair and equal arbitration, and to make a treaty and live in peace from then on.

The Argives who made these statements did so on their own authority, not by order of the people. Agis on his side accepted their proposals, and without himself consulting the majority either, simply communicated the matter to a single man, one of the high officers accompanying the expedition, and granted the Argives a four-month truce in which to make good their promises. After that he immediately led off the army without giving any explanation to any of the other allies. The Lacedaemonians and the allies followed their general out of respect for the law, but among themselves they loudly blamed Agis for going away from so fine a field — the enemy hemmed in on every side by infantry and cavalry — without having done anything worthy of their strength. This was indeed by far the finest Hellenic army ever yet brought together. It deserved to have been seen while it was still united at Nemea: the Lacedaemonians in full force, the Arcadians, Boeotians, Corinthians, Sicyonians, Pellenians, Phliasians, and Megarians — and all of these the flower of their respective populations, considering themselves a match not just for the Argive confederacy but for another like it added to it. The army withdrew, then, blaming Agis, and every man returned home. The Argives, however, blamed even more loudly the men who had concluded the truce without consulting the people, considering that they had let the Lacedaemonians escape from an opportunity such as they would never see again — since the struggle would have been under their own city walls and beside many brave allies. On their return, accordingly, they began to stone Thrasylus in the bed of the Charadrus, where they try all military cases before entering the city. Thrasylus fled to the altar and so saved his life, but his property they confiscated.

After this a thousand Athenian heavy infantry and three hundred horse arrived, under the command of Laches and Nicostratus. The Argives, still unwilling to break the truce with the Lacedaemonians, begged them to depart and refused to bring them before the people, to whom they had a communication to make, until they were forced to do so by the entreaties of the Mantineans and Eleans, who were still at Argos. The Athenians, through the mouth of Alcibiades, their ambassador on the spot, told the Argives and the allies that they had no right to make a truce at all without the consent of their fellow confederates, and that now that the Athenians had so opportunely arrived, the war ought to be resumed. These arguments succeeded with the allies, and they immediately marched on Orchomenos, all except the Argives, who, although they had consented like the rest, stayed behind at first but eventually joined the others. They all now sat down and besieged Orchomenos and made assaults on it. One of their reasons for wanting to take this place was that hostages from Arcadia had been lodged there by the Lacedaemonians. The Orchomenians, alarmed by the weakness of their wall and the size of the enemy force, and by the danger of being destroyed before relief arrived, surrendered on condition of joining the league, of giving hostages of their own to the Mantineans, and of giving up those lodged with them by the Lacedaemonians. With Orchomenos thus secured, the allies now consulted on which of the remaining places they should attack next. The Eleans pressed for Lepreum, the Mantineans for Tegea. The Argives and Athenians supported the Mantineans, and the Eleans, furious at not getting their vote for Lepreum, went home. The rest of the allies prepared at Mantinea to march against Tegea, where a faction inside had arranged to put the place into their hands.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians, on their return from Argos after the four-month truce, vehemently blamed Agis for not having subdued Argos, given an opportunity such as they thought they had never had before — for it was no easy matter to bring so many and such good allies together. But when news arrived of the capture of Orchomenos, they grew angrier than ever. Departing from all precedent, in the heat of the moment they had almost decided to raze his house and fine him ten thousand drachmae. Agis, however, begged them to do none of these things, promising to make up for his fault by good service in the field, after which they could do to him whatever they pleased. So they refrained from razing his house or fining him as they had threatened, and now made a law, previously unknown at Lacedaemon, attaching to him ten Spartans as counselors, without whose consent he was to have no power to lead an army out of the city.

At this point word arrived from their friends in Tegea that, unless they came quickly, Tegea would go over from them to the Argives and their allies, if it had not gone over already. On this news a force marched out from Lacedaemon — Spartans and Helots and all their people — at once, and on a scale never before seen. Advancing as far as Orestheum in Maenalia, they ordered the Arcadians of their league to follow close after them to Tegea. Going on themselves as far as Orestheum, they then sent home a sixth part of the Spartans, consisting of the oldest and youngest men, to guard the home country, and with the rest of their army arrived at Tegea, where their Arcadian allies soon joined them. Meanwhile they sent to Corinth, to the Boeotians, and to the Phocians and Locrians, with orders to come up as quickly as possible to Mantinea. These had short notice, and it was not easy except all together and after waiting for one another to pass through enemy country, which lay right across and blocked their line of march. Nevertheless they made what haste they could. Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians with the Arcadian allies who had joined them entered Mantinean territory, and encamping near the temple of Heracles began to plunder the country.

Here they were spotted by the Argives and their allies, who immediately took up a strong and difficult position and formed in order of battle. The Lacedaemonians at once advanced against them, and came on within a stone's throw or javelin's cast, when one of the older men, seeing that the enemy's position was a strong one, called out to Agis that he was minded to cure one evil with another — meaning that he wished to make up for his much-blamed retreat from Argos by his present untimely haste. Meanwhile Agis, whether because of this shout or because of some sudden new idea of his own, quickly led his army back without engaging, and entering Tegean territory began to divert into Mantinean territory the water that the Mantineans and Tegeans are always fighting over, on account of the heavy damage it does to whichever of the two countries it falls into. His aim was to make the Argives and their allies come down from the hill to resist the diversion of the water, as they were sure to do once they knew of it, and so to fight the battle in the plain. He accordingly stayed where he was that day, busy with diverting the water. The Argives and their allies were at first amazed at the sudden retreat of the enemy after advancing so close, and did not know what to make of it. But when he had gone away and disappeared without their having stirred to pursue him, they began once more to find fault with their generals, who had not only let the Lacedaemonians get off the time before, when they had been so neatly intercepted before Argos, but who now again allowed them to run away with no one in pursuit, and to escape at their leisure while the Argive army was leisurely betrayed. The generals, half-stunned for the moment, afterwards led the army down from the hill, advanced, and encamped in the plain, intending to attack the enemy.

The next day the Argives and their allies formed up in the order in which they intended to fight, if they happened to encounter the enemy. The Lacedaemonians, returning from the water to their old encampment by the temple of Heracles, suddenly saw their adversaries close in front of them, in full battle order, advanced from the hill. A shock like the one of that moment the Lacedaemonians do not remember ever experiencing. They had scant time for preparation, and instantly and hastily fell into their ranks, with Agis their king directing everything according to law. For when a king is in the field all commands proceed from him: he gives the word to the Polemarchs, they to the Lochages, these to the Pentecostyes, these in turn to the Enomotarchs, and these last to the Enomoties. In short, all required orders pass in the same way and reach the troops quickly — for almost the whole Lacedaemonian army, save for a small part, consists of officers under officers, and the responsibility for what is to be done falls on many.

In this battle the left wing was made up of the Sciritae, who in a Lacedaemonian army always have that post to themselves alone. Next to them were the soldiers of Brasidas from Thrace, and the Neodamodes with them. Then came the Lacedaemonians themselves, company after company, with the Arcadians of Heraea at their side. After these were the Maenalians, and on the right wing the Tegeans with a few of the Lacedaemonians at the very end. Their cavalry was posted on the two wings. Such was the Lacedaemonian formation. That of their opponents was as follows. On the right were the Mantineans, since the action took place in their country. Next to them were the allies from Arcadia. After them came the thousand picked men of the Argives, to whom the state had given a long course of military training at public expense. Next were the rest of the Argives, and after them their allies, the Cleonaeans and Orneans. Last on the extreme left were the Athenians, with their own cavalry beside them.

Such were the order and the forces of the two armies. The Lacedaemonian army looked the larger, though as for putting down the numbers of either host, or of the contingents that composed it, I could not do so with any accuracy. Owing to the secrecy of their government the number of the Lacedaemonians was not known, and men are so apt to brag about the forces of their country that the estimate by their opponents was not trusted. The following calculation, however, makes it possible to estimate the numbers of the Lacedaemonians present on this occasion. There were seven companies in the field, not counting the Sciritae, who numbered six hundred men. In each company there were four Pentecostyes, and in the Pentecosty four Enomoties. The first rank of an Enomoty was made up of four soldiers. As for the depth: although the men had not all been drawn up alike, but as each captain chose, they were generally ranged eight deep. The first rank along the whole line, exclusive of the Sciritae, consisted of four hundred and forty-eight men.

With the armies now on the eve of engaging, each contingent received words of encouragement from its own commander. The Mantineans were reminded that they were going to fight for their country, and to avoid returning to the experience of servitude after having tasted that of empire. The Argives were told that they would contend for their ancient supremacy, to regain their once equal share of the Peloponnese of which they had been so long deprived, and to punish an enemy and a neighbor for a thousand wrongs. The Athenians were urged to think of the glory of carrying off the day's honors with so many brave allies in arms, and that a victory over the Lacedaemonians in the Peloponnese would cement and extend their empire, and would also preserve Attica from any future invasion. These were the incitements addressed to the Argives and their allies. The Lacedaemonians, meanwhile, man to man, and with their war-songs in the ranks, exhorted each brave comrade to remember what he had learned before, well aware that the long training of action saves more than any brief verbal exhortation, however well delivered.

After this they joined battle. The Argives and their allies advanced with haste and fury, the Lacedaemonians slowly and to the music of many flute-players — a standing institution in their army that has nothing to do with religion, but is meant to make them advance evenly, stepping in time, without breaking their order, as large armies are apt to do at the moment of engaging.

Just before the battle was joined, King Agis decided on the following maneuver. All armies are alike in this: as they go into action they get pushed out rather to the right, and each side overlaps with this its adversary's left. Fear makes every man do his best to shelter his unarmed side with the shield of the man next to him on the right, thinking the closer the shields are locked together, the better protected he will be. The man primarily responsible for this is the one on the extreme right, who is always trying to withdraw his unarmed side from the enemy, and the same fear makes the rest follow him. On the present occasion the Mantineans extended with their wing far beyond the Sciritae, and the Lacedaemonians and Tegeans even farther beyond the Athenians, since their army was the largest. Agis, afraid of his left being surrounded, and thinking the Mantineans outflanked it too far, ordered the Sciritae and Brasideans to move out from their place in the ranks and make the line even with the Mantineans. He told the Polemarchs Hipponoidas and Aristocles to fill the gap thus formed by throwing themselves into it with two companies taken from the right wing, thinking his right would still be strong enough and to spare, and that the line facing the Mantineans would gain in solidity.

However, since he gave these orders in the moment of the onset and at short notice, it so happened that Aristocles and Hipponoidas would not move over — for which offence they were afterwards banished from Sparta on the charge of cowardice. Meanwhile the enemy closed before the Sciritae (whom Agis, on seeing that the two companies did not move over, ordered to return to their place) had time to fill the breach in question. Now it was, however, that the Lacedaemonians, completely outdone in skill, showed themselves all the more superior in courage. As soon as they came to close quarters with the enemy, the Mantinean right broke their Sciritae and Brasideans, and bursting in with their allies and the thousand picked Argives into the unclosed gap in the line, cut up and surrounded the Lacedaemonians and drove them in full rout to the wagons, killing some of the older men on guard there. But the Lacedaemonians, beaten in this part of the field, with the rest of their army, and especially the center where the three hundred knights, as they are called, fought around King Agis, fell on the older men of the Argives and the so-called five companies, on the Cleonaeans and Orneans, and on the Athenians next to them, and instantly routed them. Most did not even wait to strike a blow, but gave way the moment the Lacedaemonians came on; some were even trampled underfoot in their fear of being overtaken by their assailants.

The army of the Argives and their allies, having given way at this point, was now completely cut in two. The Lacedaemonian and Tegean right simultaneously closed around the Athenians with the troops that outflanked them, and the Athenians found themselves caught between two fires, surrounded on one side and already defeated on the other. Indeed they would have suffered more severely than any other part of the army, but for the services of the cavalry they had with them. Agis, on perceiving the distress of his left wing opposed to the Mantineans and the thousand Argives, ordered the whole army to advance to the support of the defeated wing. While this was going on, as the enemy moved past and slanted away from them, the Athenians escaped at their leisure, and with them the beaten Argive division. Meanwhile the Mantineans and their allies and the picked body of the Argives ceased pressing the enemy, and seeing their friends defeated and the Lacedaemonians in full advance on them, took to flight. Many of the Mantineans fell, but the bulk of the picked Argive body got safely away. The flight and retreat, however, were neither hurried nor long. The Lacedaemonians fight long and stubbornly until they rout an enemy, but once that is done they pursue for only a short distance.

Such was the battle, as nearly as I can give it — the greatest that had occurred among the Hellenes for a very long time, and one in which the most considerable states took part. The Lacedaemonians took up a position in front of the enemy's dead, immediately set up a trophy, and stripped the slain. They took up their own dead and carried them back to Tegea, where they buried them, and gave back those of the enemy under truce. The Argives, Orneans, and Cleonaeans had seven hundred killed; the Mantineans two hundred; and the Athenians and Aeginetans also two hundred, with both their generals. On the side of the Lacedaemonians, the allies suffered no loss worth mentioning. As for the Lacedaemonians themselves, the truth was difficult to learn, but it is said that about three hundred of them fell.

While the battle was impending, Pleistoanax, the other king, set out with a reinforcement of the oldest and youngest men, and got as far as Tegea, where he heard of the victory and went back. The Lacedaemonians also sent and turned back the allies coming from Corinth and from beyond the Isthmus, and on returning home themselves dismissed their allies and kept the Carnean holidays, which happened to fall just then. The accusations brought against them by the Hellenes at the time — whether of cowardice on account of the disaster on the island, or of mismanagement and slowness generally — were all wiped out by this single action. Fortune, it was thought, might have humbled them, but the men themselves were the same as ever.

The day before this battle, the Epidaurians invaded the deserted Argive territory with their full forces, and cut off many of the guards left there in the absence of the Argive army. After the battle, three thousand Elean heavy infantry arrived to help the Mantineans, with a reinforcement of a thousand Athenians. All these allies marched at once against Epidaurus, while the Lacedaemonians were keeping the Carnea, and dividing the work among themselves began to build a wall around the city. The rest gave it up, but the Athenians at once finished the section assigned to them around Cape Heraeum. Together they left a garrison in the fortification in question and returned to their respective cities.

Summer now came to an end. In the first days of the following winter, when the Carnean holidays were over, the Lacedaemonians took the field, and on reaching Tegea sent on to Argos proposals of accommodation. They had previously had a party in the town that wanted to overthrow the democracy, and after the recent battle these were now in a much better position to persuade the people to listen to terms. Their plan was first to make a treaty with the Lacedaemonians, then an alliance, and after that to fall on the commons. Lichas, son of Arcesilaus, the Argive proxenus, accordingly arrived at Argos with two proposals from Lacedaemon, regulating the conditions of war or peace, according to which they preferred. After much discussion — Alcibiades happening to be in the town — the Lacedaemonian party, who now ventured to act openly, persuaded the Argives to accept the proposal for accommodation, which ran as follows:
The assembly of the Lacedaemonians agrees to treat with the Argives upon the following terms:
1. The Argives shall restore to the Orchomenians their children, and to the Maenalians their men, and shall restore the men they hold in Mantinea to the Lacedaemonians.

2. They shall evacuate Epidaurus and raze the fortification there. If the Athenians refuse to withdraw from Epidaurus, they shall be declared enemies of the Argives and of the Lacedaemonians, and of the allies of the Lacedaemonians and the allies of the Argives.
3. If the Lacedaemonians have any children in their custody, they shall restore each one of them to his city.
4. As to the offering to the god, the Argives may, if they wish, impose an oath on the Epidaurians, but if not, they shall swear it themselves.
5. All the cities in the Peloponnese, both small and great, shall be independent according to the customs of their country.
6. If any of the powers outside the Peloponnese invades Peloponnesian territory, the contracting parties shall unite to repel them, on whatever terms they may agree as fairest for the Peloponnesians.

7. All allies of the Lacedaemonians outside the Peloponnese shall be on the same footing as the Lacedaemonians, and the allies of the Argives shall be on the same footing as the Argives, each being left in possession of their own.
8. This treaty shall be shown to the allies, and shall be concluded if they approve. If the allies think fit, they may send the treaty to be considered at home.

The Argives began by accepting this proposal, and the Lacedaemonian army returned home from Tegea. After this, normal relations between them were resumed, and not long afterwards the same party arranged for the Argives to give up the league with the Mantineans, Eleans, and Athenians, and to make a treaty and alliance with the Lacedaemonians. This was done on the following terms:
The Lacedaemonians and Argives agree to a treaty and alliance for fifty years upon the following terms:
1. All disputes shall be decided by fair and impartial arbitration, in accordance with the customs of the two countries.

2. The rest of the cities in the Peloponnese may be included in this treaty and alliance, as independent and sovereign, in full possession of what they have, all disputes being decided by fair and impartial arbitration in accordance with the customs of the said cities.

3. All allies of the Lacedaemonians outside the Peloponnese shall be on the same footing as the Lacedaemonians themselves, and the allies of the Argives shall be on the same footing as the Argives themselves, each continuing to possess what they have.
4. If it should anywhere be necessary to make a joint expedition, the Lacedaemonians and Argives shall consult on it and decide as is fairest for the allies.

5. If any of the cities, whether inside or outside the Peloponnese, have a question of borders or anything else, it must be settled. If one allied city should have a quarrel with another allied city, it must be referred to some third city judged impartial by both parties. Private citizens shall have their disputes decided according to the laws of their several countries.

Once the treaty and alliance were concluded, each party at once released everything taken whether by war or otherwise, and thenceforth, acting in common, they voted to receive neither herald nor embassy from the Athenians unless the Athenians evacuated their forts and withdrew from the Peloponnese, and also to make neither peace nor war with anyone except jointly. Zeal was not lacking: both parties sent envoys to the Thracian places and to Perdiccas, and persuaded the latter to join their league. He did not, however, at once break with Athens, although he was minded to do so on seeing the way shown him by Argos, the original home of his family. They also renewed their old oaths with the Chalcidians and took new ones. The Argives, in addition, sent ambassadors to the Athenians, bidding them evacuate the fort at Epidaurus. The Athenians, seeing their own men outnumbered by the rest of the garrison, sent Demosthenes to bring them out. This general, under cover of a gymnastic contest which he arranged on his arrival, got the rest of the garrison out of the place and shut the gates behind them. The Athenians later renewed their treaty with the Epidaurians and on their own gave up the fortress.

After the defection of Argos from the league, the Mantineans, although they held out at first, in the end found themselves powerless without the Argives, and they too came to terms with Lacedaemon, and gave up their sovereignty over the towns. The Lacedaemonians and Argives, a thousand strong each, now took the field together. The Lacedaemonians first went by themselves to Sicyon and made the government there more oligarchical than before, and then both, uniting, put down the democracy at Argos and set up an oligarchy favorable to Lacedaemon. These events occurred at the close of the winter, just before spring, and the fourteenth year of the war ended. The next summer the people of Dium, in Athos, revolted from the Athenians to the Chalcidians, and the Lacedaemonians settled affairs in Achaea in a way more agreeable to the interests of their country. Meanwhile the popular party at Argos little by little regained consistency and courage, and waited for the moment of the Gymnopaedic festival at Lacedaemon, and then fell on the oligarchs. After a fight in the city, victory went to the commons, who killed some of their opponents and banished others. The Lacedaemonians for a long while let the messages of their friends at Argos remain unanswered. At last they postponed the Gymnopaediae and marched to their assistance. But on learning at Tegea of the defeat of the oligarchs, they refused to go any further, in spite of the entreaties of those who had escaped, and returned home and kept the festival. Later on envoys arrived with messages from the Argives in the city and from the exiles, while the allies were also at Sparta. After much had been said on both sides, the Lacedaemonians decided that the party in the city had done wrong, and resolved to march against Argos, but kept delaying and putting off the matter. Meanwhile the commons at Argos, in fear of the Lacedaemonians, began once again to court the Athenian alliance, which they were convinced would be of the greatest service to them. They accordingly began to build long walls to the sea, so that, in case of a blockade by land, with the help of the Athenians they might have the advantage of importing what they wanted by sea. Some of the cities in the Peloponnese were also in on the building of these walls. The Argives, with all their people — including women and slaves — set themselves to the work, while carpenters and masons came to them from Athens.

Summer was now over. The following winter the Lacedaemonians, hearing of the walls being built, marched against Argos with their allies, the Corinthians excepted, having also some intelligence within the city itself. Agis, son of Archidamus, their king, was in command. The intelligence they had counted on inside the town came to nothing. They did, however, take and raze the walls being built, and after capturing the Argive town of Hysiae and killing all the free men that fell into their hands, they went back and every man dispersed to his city. After this the Argives marched into Phlius and plundered it for harboring their exiles, most of whom had settled there, and then returned home. The same winter the Athenians blockaded Macedonia, on the grounds of the league entered into by Perdiccas with the Argives and Lacedaemonians, and also of his breach of engagements on the occasion of the expedition prepared by Athens against the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace and against Amphipolis, under the command of Nicias, son of Niceratus — which had had to be broken up mainly because of his desertion. He was therefore proclaimed an enemy. And so the winter ended, and the fifteenth year of the war ended with it.
